title: Chapter VIII
focus: injustice and the burden of silence

teacherSummary.text: Justine is tried. Though innocent, she confesses under pressure from her confessor, who threatened her with damnation, and is executed. Elizabeth defends her eloquently; Victor suffers privately but does not speak.

vocabulary.definition: To soil, or change the appearance of, especially by an alternation induced by the air, or by dust, or the like
vocabulary.context: Elizabeth also wept, and was unhappy; but hers also was the misery of innocence, which, like a cloud that passes over the fair moon, for a while hides but cannot tarnish its brightness.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “tarnish”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.definition: To cheer in distress or depression
vocabulary.context: I soon shall see you again in heaven, where we shall all be happy; and that consoles me, going as I am to suffer ignominy and death.”
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “console”: con- (Latin com-, "with, together") + sol (Latin solus, "alone" / sol, "sun"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.context: I passed a night of unmingled wretchedness.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “unmingle”: un- (Old English un-, "not") + min (Latin minor, "smaller"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.definition: A companion in amusements or sports
vocabulary.context: You shall not die!—You, my playfellow, my companion, my sister, perish on the scaffold!
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “playfellow”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.definition: To strike together, as in anger or pain
vocabulary.context: I gnashed my teeth, and ground them together, uttering a groan that came from my inmost soul.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “gnash”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.context: Elizabeth’s heartrending eloquence failed to move the judges from their settled conviction in the criminality of the saintly sufferer.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “heartrending”: -ing (Old English -ing, action). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: To move away from the position occupied
vocabulary.context: It removes more than half my misfortune; and I feel as if I could die in peace, now that my innocence is acknowledged by you, dear lady, and your cousin.”
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “remove”: re- (Latin re-, "back, again") + mov (Latin movere, "to move"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.definition: To feel absence of trust in
vocabulary.context: “Oh, Justine! forgive me for having for one moment distrusted you.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “distrust”: dis- (Latin dis-, "apart, not"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: The act of communicating or ejecting
vocabulary.context: He threatened excommunication and hell fire in my last moments, if I continued obdurate.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “excommunication”: ex- (Latin ex, "out of") + -ation (Latin -atio, "the act or result of"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: To write underneath, as one's name
vocabulary.context: In an evil hour I subscribed to a lie; and now only am I truly miserable.”
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “subscribe”: sub- (Latin sub, "under") + scrib (Latin scribere, "to write"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

context.history: Courts of the time could convict on circumstantial evidence; religious confession carried enormous social pressure.

significance: Justice fails, showing how society punishes the vulnerable while the guilty (Victor, indirectly) remain free.

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: In “Chapter VIII,” how does Shelley show injustice and the burden of silence? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the irony you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: High School / Common Core
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Chapter VIII develops the idea of injustice and the burden of silence. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of irony and characterization shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Mary Shelley uses irony in Chapter VIII to complicate the reader's understanding of injustice and the burden of silence. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Chapter VIII within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of injustice and the burden of silence responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Chapter VIII as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of injustice and the burden of silence. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Frankenstein.

segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: Who is responsible for Justine's death? Rank the characters and defend your order. No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board.

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script: Today's words are tarnish, consoles, unmingled, playfellow, gnashed. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check Webster's. Here is the first: “Elizabeth also wept, and was unhappy; but hers also was the misery of innocence, which, like a cloud that passes over the fair moon, for a while hides but cannot tarnish its brightness.” Webster's says: To soil, or change the appearance of, especially by an alternation induced by the air, or by dust, or the like. Now the word history: “tarnish”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin. “console”: con- (Latin com-, "with, together") + sol (Latin solus, "alone" / sol, "sun"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary. “unmingle”: un- (Old English un-, "not") + min (Latin minor, "smaller"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary. Add each root to your etymology log.

segments.activity: Present the historical and literary background.
segments.script: Here is what the first readers of Frankenstein would have known. Courts of the time could convict on circumstantial evidence; religious confession carried enormous social pressure. Why does this chapter matter? Justice fails, showing how society punishes the vulnerable while the guilty (Victor, indirectly) remain free. Write down one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Teacher models a think-aloud on the anchor passage for irony.
segments.script: Watch me read this the way a careful reader does. I read a sentence, stop, and ask what the author is doing. When I see irony, I underline it and write in the margin what effect it has. Here I notice the diction and the sentence rhythm, and I connect them to injustice and the burden of silence.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for Irony, Characterization, Theme.
segments.script: Now we do it together. I read the first sentence and you track along. Mark every example of irony. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice? I will collect three ideas and we choose the strongest using evidence.
segments.passage: I passed a night of unmingled wretchedness. In the morning I went to the court; my lips and throat were parched. I dared not ask the fatal question; but I was known, and the officer guessed the cause of my visit. The ballots had been thrown; they were all black, and Justine was condemned.

segments.activity: Students annotate a new passage independently in the reader, then begin the writing prompt at their rigor.
segments.script: Your turn. Annotate the next page in the app for Irony, Characterization, Theme: at least three marks with a margin note each. Then open your writing prompt; your level is already set. Middle-school version: In “Chapter VIII,” how does Shelley show injustice and the burden of silence? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the irony you noticed as one piece of evidence. I will circulate and conference.

segments.activity: Structured discussion (think-pair-share or a short Socratic circle).
segments.script: Let's talk. Our question: How does this chapter connect to the costs of unchecked ambition? Every claim needs a page reference. Respond to the person before you by agreeing, extending or challenging with evidence.

segments.activity: Chapter quiz in the app, then a one-sentence exit ticket.
segments.script: Take the chapter quiz in the app. Then, in one sentence, tell me what this chapter suggests about injustice and the burden of silence, backed by one short quotation.

segments.activity: Summarize the lesson and preview the next reading.
segments.script: Today we saw how irony shapes injustice and the burden of silence. Tonight, read the next chapter and add two words to your etymology log.
